$comment: Tests that fail on a headless server for a reason that is not a bug, with
the reason. `npm run bds:test` reads this: a test listed here is allowed to
fail, and one that PASSES fails the run, because that means the reason has
expired and the entry should go. The long version is in README.md and
Add an entry only for a result that is evidence about the HARNESS. A test
that fails because the pack does not do what it says belongs in a GitHub
issue, failing, until it is fixed.
anchor_sets_spawn: A SimulatedPlayer marshals as undefined into any pack that does not itself bind @minecraft/server-gametest, so Hearthstone never sees the anchor's placer - and a SimulatedPlayer spawns with a spawn point already set, which Hearthstone correctly treats as foreign and refuses to touch. Measured; Hearthstone is right and the test cannot be written this way.
rain_collector: weatherChange never fires on a headless server. Measured with a module-scope subscription in the probe pack (qolprobe W1), which logs every event and needs no player: nothing is reported for a scripted setWeather, for the console's own `weather rain`, or with a SimulatedPlayer present. Fluidworks can only learn the weather from that event - Dimension.getWeather is beta-only - so ctx.raining is never true here and the tank is never filled. This says nothing about whether the rain collector works in a real session, where real weather cycles do fire it; that is in the Fluidworks README to confirm in game.
keep_on_death_stops_the_drop: A SimulatedPlayer killed and respawned on a headless server keeps its whole inventory, flagged or not. The test carries two stacks and flags only one, exactly so a world that never drops cannot be mistaken for the flag working: both come back, twice, run alone. It is not the gamerule - keepinventory reads 0 in the test world's level.dat - so nothing the harness can set makes this measurable, and the assertion that fails is the control. The same blindness makes death_keeps_items green for a reason that is not Graves working; the probe pack's qolprobe:death and qolprobe:keepflag are how a real player settles it. Keep the test: it fails loudly with the measurement in the message, and it is the one line that would notice if the engine ever started dropping a simulated player's items.
dispenser_washes_leather: The wash rule's happy path cannot be reached from a headless server, for two measured reasons that compound. A leather helmet built by script carries no minecraft:dyeable component at all - the same shape as the food components only data-driven items have - so readItemColor sees no colour and the rule correctly refuses it. And a SimulatedPlayer cannot dye one in the world either: four uses of a helmet on a cauldron of dyed water leave the component undefined, which is the cauldron swallowing a simulated player's click again (docs/README.md corrections). So there is no way to hand the machine a dyed item here. The refusal half IS measured, by dispenser_leaves_undyed_leather_alone: nothing to wash off costs no water. Whether a real player's dyed armour comes back clean, named and enchanted is for a session in game; this test is kept, failing, because it is the full path and it starts passing the moment either half becomes possible.
